source.text: Ce matin, il pleuvait sur la ville. Les gens marchaient vite, cachés sous leurs parapluies. Malgré le mauvais temps, un vieux monsieur souriait dans sa boutique. « La pluie fait pousser les fleurs », disait-il souvent.

sentences.text: Ce matin, il pleuvait sur la ville.
sentences.translation: This morning, it was raining over the city.

sentences.text: Les gens marchaient vite, cachés sous leurs parapluies.
sentences.translation: People were walking quickly, sheltered under their umbrellas.

sentences.text: Malgré le mauvais temps, un vieux monsieur souriait dans sa boutique.
sentences.translation: Despite the bad weather, an elderly gentleman was smiling in his shop.

sentences.text: « La pluie fait pousser les fleurs », disait-il souvent.
sentences.translation: “Rain makes the flowers grow,” he often said.
sentences.literal: “The rain makes grow the flowers,” he said often.

vocabulary.meaningInContext: it was raining (impersonal weather verb, only ever used with 'il')
collocations: il pleut des cordes (it's raining hard)

examples.text: Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti.
examples.translation: It was raining when I went out.

vocabulary.meaningInContext: sheltering / hidden (past participle of 'cacher', used as an adjective describing 'les gens')

morphology.description: past participle of 'cacher', agreeing in masculine plural with 'les gens'

collocations: ouvrir un parapluie (to open an umbrella)

examples.text: Malgré la pluie, ils sont sortis.
examples.translation: Despite the rain, they went out.

commonErrors: do not write 'malgré que'; use 'bien que' + subjunctive instead

vocabulary.meaningInContext: to grow; here in 'faire pousser', to make (flowers) grow

examples.text: On annonce du mauvais temps pour demain.
examples.translation: Bad weather is forecast for tomorrow.

grammar.title: L'imparfait — the background/ongoing past
grammar.explanation: The imparfait describes an ongoing state or background scene in the past. In this text it sets the scene: 'il pleuvait' (it was raining), 'marchaient' (they were walking), 'souriait' (he was smiling). It contrasts with the passé composé, which reports completed events.

examples.translation: It was raining over the city.

pitfalls: using the passé composé to describe background states
forgetting the imparfait for habitual actions (used to)

grammar.title: The past participle as an adjective (agreement)
grammar.explanation: A past participle can modify a noun like an adjective. Here 'cachés' describes 'les gens' and agrees with it in masculine plural (-s).
grammar.pattern: noun + past participle (agreeing in gender and number)

examples.text: Les gens, cachés sous leurs parapluies, marchaient vite.
examples.translation: The people, sheltered under their umbrellas, walked quickly.

pitfalls: forgetting the agreement when the participle modifies a preceding noun

grammar.title: The causative 'faire + infinitive'
grammar.explanation: 'faire' + infinitive means 'to make/have something happen'. 'La pluie fait pousser les fleurs' = 'the rain makes the flowers grow'. The subject (la pluie) causes the action; the doer of the infinitive, if expressed, becomes an indirect object (à…).
pitfalls: using the wrong pronoun for the doer of the action

exercises.prompt: In this sentence, what does « malgré » mean?

answer.explanation: « malgré » introduces a concession: despite the bad weather.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Ce matin, il ___ sur la ville.

answer.explanation: The imparfait 'pleuvait' describes the ongoing rain that set the scene.

exercises.prompt: Which past tense is used in « il pleuvait »?

answer.explanation: The imparfait describes the background state of the weather.

exercises.prompt: Translate into English: « La pluie fait pousser les fleurs. »

rubric: renders the causative 'faire + infinitive' as 'make(s) … grow'
keeps 'la pluie' as the subject and 'les fleurs' as the object
answer.explanation: The causative construction 'faire pousser' means 'to make grow'.

exercises.prompt: Which adjective forms the collocation for 'bad weather' in the text?

answer.explanation: 'mauvais temps' is the standard collocation for 'bad weather'.
